b: Bringing a dog into your life is a huge responsibility. This usually changes how you and your household manage daily routines, spending, and free time outside of work. Following up on her wonderful book titled Who’s a Good Dog? And How to Be a Better Human, dog expert and bioethicist Dr. Jessica Pierce flips the coin in her new book titled Who’s a Good Human? Practical Exercises for Living Mindfully with Dogs and focuses on how we might change our own behavior—rather than trying to change our household companion. Pierce wants to cultivate a more curious, collaborative, and compassionate relationship with the dogs they love.
Marc Bekoff: Why did you write Who’s a Good Human?

Jessica Pierce: We spend a lot of time asking whether dogs are “good”—whether they behave properly, follow our rules, and fit comfortably into human lives. But what happens when we turn that question around and ask what it means to be a good human in our relationships with dogs?

Dogs are a particularly rich place to begin thinking about this question because they live so intimately with us. We decide on nearly every aspect of their lives—where they go, what they eat, who they see, when they sleep, how they behave, and how much freedom they have. We love them deeply, and yet our care can also constrain them in ways we don't always notice.

The book invites us to shift our perception—to see dogs differently, and to see ourselves differently in relation to them. Part of becoming a better human is learning to notice things that didn't seem important: a dog's hesitation, a preference, a small gesture of communication, an opportunity for choice, or the ways our own habits shape a dog's world. The book is partly about changing our moral perception—changing what and who we notice, what we consider ethically significant, and what calls for our attention and care.
MB: How does your book relate to your background and general areas of interest?

JP: Who’s a Good Human? brings together many of the threads that have run through my work as a bioethicist, philosopher, and writer: animal ethics, care, relationships, attention, embodiment, agency, and the question of how we might live responsibly with other beings.

My work with dogs has increasingly convinced me that ethics isn't only about what principles we endorse or what rules we follow. It's also about what we are capable of perceiving. We can't respond ethically to something we don't notice, and we often fail to notice precisely because our habits and cultural assumptions have taught us that certain things don't matter.

Dogs make this especially visible because they are constantly communicating with us, but we don't always recognize what they are saying. We may interpret a dog's behavior through the lens of obedience, convenience, or human expectations rather than asking what the behavior might tell us about the dog's experience.

MB: Who is your intended audience?
JP: I hope it will be useful to trainers, veterinarians, behavior professionals, animal advocates, educators, and anyone interested in animal ethics and human-animal relationships.
MB: What are some of the topics you weave into your book, and what are some of your major messages?

JP: The book explores the idea that becoming a better human begins, in part, with learning to see differently. I ask readers to examine their assumptions about dogs and pay attention to the things that tend to disappear into the background of everyday life.

The workbook exercises are designed to make these shifts in perception tangible. I ask readers to observe their own behavior through an ethogram, think about communication through a bark ethogram, examine the choices available to themselves and their dogs, and to experiment with things like taking a walk without a predetermined human agenda. These exercises are simple, but they can disrupt habitual ways of seeing.

A major theme is moral salience: What comes into focus as something that matters morally? We tend to notice some kinds of suffering very readily while overlooking others. We may recognize obvious physical pain in a dog but fail to notice chronic frustration, boredom, lack of agency, social isolation, or the cumulative effects of having very little control over one's daily life. We may think a dog's preference as trivial when we would regard a similar preference in a human as meaningful.

I want readers to become more sensitive to these quieter dimensions of animal experience. That doesn't mean assuming that dogs are just like humans or projecting our own experiences onto them. Quite the opposite: It means becoming more curious about dogs as dogs.

And there is an important paradox here. The more closely we attend to dogs as individuals, the less satisfying simple rules about “good” and “bad” behavior become. We start to see particular dogs with particular histories, preferences, capacities, vulnerabilities, and ways of engaging with the world.

The book isn't a manual for becoming a perfect dog guardian. It invites readers to practice a different kind of attention—to become more perceptive, more curious, and more willing to have our assumptions challenged.
MB: Are you hopeful that as people become more attentive to their own behavior and their relationships with dogs, they will become better humans?

JP: Yes. What gives me hope is the possibility of practice. We can practice noticing. We can practice curiosity. We can practice seeing from a perspective other than our own. And as our perception changes, our sense of what matters can change with it.

Dogs offer an extraordinary opportunity for this kind of practice because they are so close to us and yet so different from us. They constantly invite us to negotiate the world with another kind of being. If we learn to take their experiences seriously—not simply because they are cute or beloved, but because they are sentient individuals with their own ways of experiencing and moving through the world—we may begin to develop habits of attention that extend beyond our relationships with dogs.

That is where I think the larger ethical possibility lies. A shift in how we see one dog can become a shift in what we notice in other animals, and eventually a shift in how we understand ourselves as participants in multispecies worlds.

For me, being a good human isn't a status we achieve. It's an ongoing practice of noticing, questioning, responding, and sometimes changing course. The goal isn't to get everything right. It's to become the kind of person who is increasingly able to see what—and who—matters.

In conversation with Dr. Jessica Pierce, an internationally acclaimed bioethicist and writer whose work focuses on animals, ethics, and the everyday ways humans can learn to live more thoughtfully with other species. She has published fourteen books, including Morality Play: Case Studies in Ethics, A Dog’s World: Imagining the Lives of Dogs in a World without Humans, and, most recently, Dogpedia: A Brief Compendium of Canine Curiosities. Her essays have appeared in The New York Times, The Washington Post, The Guardian, TIME, and Scientific American.
